title: Loop Engineering
text:
Loop
Engineering
Let the last result guide the next step.
A workshop for everyday engineering work



TRIGGER
Agent
VERIFY
LOOP ENGINEERING
01
notes:
Think about the last task you gave a coding agent.
It made a change. You checked the work. Then you had to tell it what to do next.
Today, we will look at how to arrange those next steps in advance.
The aim is to let the work continue using evidence, with clear places to stop and review.
Next slide:
Before we look at an example, let me briefly explain the kind of work I do.

title: Harshit Tyagi
text:
Harshit Tyagi
AI Consultant & Founder · Agentiwise



I turn agent prototypes into reliable systems that create business value.

I founded glued.me, a marketing SaaS built around agents.

I teach practical AI through O'Reilly, LinkedIn Learning, YouTube, and consulting.

I focus on systems people can inspect and improve.
LOOP ENGINEERING
02
notes:
I build agent systems for everyday work, and I teach engineers how to make those systems useful.
A large part of that work starts after the first answer arrives.
We need to understand what happened, check the change, and decide what should happen next.
Next slide:
Let me show you a small failure that creates exactly this kind of work.

title: Why did the assistant lose the topic?
text:
Why did the assistant lose the topic?

LOOP ENGINEERING
3
“How should we handle duplicate webhook deliveries?”
“What should I do next?”
The approved webhook article exists. The search misses it.
notes:
A customer asks how to handle duplicate webhook deliveries.
Then they ask a perfectly normal follow-up: ‘What should I do next?’
The search uses that short message on its own. It loses the earlier topic.
The approved webhook article exists, but the search misses it.
Next slide:
Who now has to figure out what went wrong and what the agent should try next?

title: What work does that failure create?
text:
What work does that failure create?

LOOP ENGINEERING
4
Understand the failure
Read the question, the search query, and the returned sources.

Request a change
Ask the coding agent for a small fix. Run the checks again.

Do it again later
Review the patch. Repeat the checking when a new question arrives.
notes:
An engineer reads the question and opens the search trace.
They ask the coding agent for a change. Then they run the checks and inspect the patch.
When another question arrives, someone has to pick up that work again.
Much of the effort is in carrying the work from one decision to the next.
Next slide:
Could we decide how those handoffs should work before we start?

title: What are we engineering around the agent?
text:
What are we engineering around the agent?

LOOP ENGINEERING
5
A way to use the last result
to choose the next allowed action.
Give it evidence
A check that shows what changed and what still needs work.

Decide when it should try again, wait for review, or stop.
notes:
That is what we are designing when we build a loop.
We give the agent a result to reach and a way to check the current state.
We say what it may change.
Then we decide how the last result should lead to another attempt, a review, or a stop.
Next slide:
What would that look like with a task most engineering teams recognise?

title: How does a result guide the next attempt?
text:
How does a result guide the next attempt?

LOOP ENGINEERING
06
Make a slow test suite faster

Measure
Time the full suite

Change one cause
Shared setup or slow I/O

Recheck
Same tests, same runner

Still too slow? The timing result becomes the next instruction.
notes:
Take a slow test suite.
We time the full suite, find one cause of the delay, and make a small change.
Then we run the same suite again.
If the tests pass but it is still too slow, the new timing tells us where to look next.
The result of one attempt becomes useful input for the next attempt.
Next slide:
What tells this loop when to begin?

title: When should the work start again?
text:
When should the work start again?

LOOP ENGINEERING
07
Manual
You submit a goal.
The full test suite is 20% faster.

Scheduled
The hourly check fires.
Docs match verified shipped changes.

After an alert
A fixed log export arrives.
Each reproducible group has a passing test.
notes:
Sometimes we start it ourselves by submitting a goal.
Sometimes a schedule starts another check, such as an hourly check for documentation changes.
Sometimes new evidence arrives after an alert. An engineer can hand over a fixed log export and start the work.
Once a run starts, it may need several attempts. Starting a new run later is a separate choice.
Next slide:
Which of these ideas are we going to apply to our support assistant?

title: Which loop are we building?
text:
Which loop are we building?

LOOP ENGINEERING
8
The support assistant
Find approved articles and answer a customer.

The engineering loop
Check examples. Request a code change. Check again. Wait for review.

A new question starts a fresh check of that same system.
notes:
The support assistant has one job: find approved articles and answer the customer.
We are building an engineering loop around that assistant.
This outer loop checks saved questions, asks for a small code change when needed, and checks the system again.
A useful change waits for review. New questions can start fresh checks later.
Next slide:
How will we know whether one of those changes helped?

title: What would count as better?
text:
What would count as better?

LOOP ENGINEERING
09
Checks with a clear rule
Checks that need judgment

The same full test suite still passes.
•
The expected article ranks first.
•
Tests and assertions stay intact.
•
Docs match shipped product behavior.
•
RAG claims follow approved evidence.
•
A judge agrees with reviewed examples.
•

Stop on success, a budget limit, a regression, or a need for human judgment.
notes:
We need to agree on the evidence before we start changing things.
Some checks have a clear rule. The tests pass. The expected article appears first.
Other checks need judgment. An answer can find the right article and still miss an important detail.
For our hands-on example, the automatic check will cover finding the expected source. We will review answer quality separately.
Next slide:
With that distinction in mind, where does another attempt create useful work?

title: Where does another attempt help?
text:
Where does another attempt help?

LOOP ENGINEERING
10
Speed up the test suite
Time it. Fix one slow cause. Time the same suite again.
Timing evidence

Sync docs with shipped code
Find one verified mismatch. Update it. Recheck the list.
Mismatch list

Work through an error window
Reproduce one group. Fix its cause. Retest what remains.
Remaining errors
notes:
Look at these jobs through the work that remains.
A timing profile points to the next slow cause. A list of documentation mismatches points to the next verified edit.
A fixed error window gives us another reproducible group to investigate.
A loop helps when the last check tells us something useful about what to do next.
Next slide:
What do we need to write down before letting that work continue?
Presenter cue:
Keep this slide brief. Slide 7 explained when work starts. This slide explains why another attempt helps.

title: What must the loop know before it starts?
text:
What must the loop know before it starts?

LOOP ENGINEERING
11
1
Trigger
What starts this run?

2
Goal
What result are we trying to reach?

3
Action
What is the next allowed change?

4
Check state
What happened, and what will the next run read?

5
Stop
When do we finish, pause, or ask a person?

Five choices for the run. Next, we will connect them through feedback.
notes:
We need five clear answers.
What starts the run? What result are we trying to reach? What may the agent change?
What will it check and save? When should it stop or wait for someone?
These choices will appear in the prompts, the feedback diagram, and the hands-on example. We are looking at the same loop in more detail.
Next slide:
What does this look like as a prompt we could actually run?

title: How would you ask for a faster test suite?
text:
How would you ask for a faster test suite?

Start once with /goal. Replace the highlighted fields for your project.
LOOP ENGINEERING
12
Goal
/goal Make the full test suite at least [20%] faster.
Trigger
Start when I submit this goal.
Action
Record the median of [3] full runs on the same runner.
Profile the slowest work. Change one shared cause.
Check + save
Rerun the same suite [3] times after each change.
Keep changes only when tests pass and timing improves.
Preserve every test, assertion, fixture, and coverage target.
Save timings, the diff, and the next idea in [loop-state.md].
Repeat + stop
Repeat until the [20%] improvement is verified.
Stop after [3 changes] or [25 minutes], or if blocked.
Leave a local diff for review. Do not merge or deploy.
notes:
Here is the slow-test example written as an agreement with the agent.
We set a target, measure the same full suite, and ask it to work on one cause at a time.
The tests and assertions stay fixed. After every change, it repeats the measurement and saves what happened.
The highlighted fields are the values we would replace for our own project.
The last lines say when the work ends and what the reviewer should receive.
Next slide:
How would those instructions change if new work arrived every hour?
Presenter cue:
Walk through the goal, the fixed check, and the stop condition. Let learners read the remaining lines or use the copyable prompt page.

title: How would the docs loop find new work?
text:
How would the docs loop find new work?

Claude Code /loop. Replace the highlighted fields before starting.
LOOP ENGINEERING
13
Goal + interval
/loop [1h] Check shipped changes since [docs-loop-state.json].
Trigger
Run hourly while this session is open.
Action
List documentation that disagrees with those shipped changes.
Update one verified mismatch. Build docs and check links.
Check + save
Repeat within this pass until the list is empty.
If a docs diff awaits review, skip this pass.
Leave unclear product claims for a person to review.
Save the checked commit, remaining items, and test results.
Stop
Stop each pass after [3 edits] or [15 minutes].
If there is no work, make no edits. Do not publish.
Cancel this recurring task after [3 passes].
notes:
Now the schedule starts a fresh pass through the documentation work.
Within that pass, the agent works through verified mismatches one at a time.
It saves the last checked commit and anything still unresolved, so the next pass can continue from known state.
If there is no new work, it makes no edit. If a change already waits for review, it waits too.
Next slide:
What if the starting evidence comes from an alert instead of a schedule?

title: How would a loop work through errors?
text:
How would a loop work through errors?

An alert supplies logs. An engineer starts /goal with the fixed export.
LOOP ENGINEERING
14
Goal
/goal Resolve reproducible errors in [logs/error-window.json].
Trigger
Start after an alert supplies this fixed log export.
Action
Group duplicates. Select one high-impact reproducible group.
Reproduce it locally. Add a failing test. Fix one shared cause.
Check + save
Rerun that test and the full suite after each change.
Repeat for the remaining groups in this same log window.
Save the reproduction, diff, and test results.
Report external failures separately. Do not call them fixed.
Stop
Stop when all reproducible groups pass their tests.
Stop after [3 fixes] or [25 minutes], or on an unclear cause.
Leave a local diff. Do not change production or deploy.
notes:
An alert gives us a fixed window of errors. An engineer starts the goal with that log export.
The agent groups duplicates, reproduces one useful case, adds a failing test, and changes one cause.
Then it reruns the checks and looks at the remaining groups.
A clear limit keeps this investigation small enough to inspect.
Next slide:
These examples use different inputs. What is the common mechanism underneath them?

title: How does feedback guide the next action?
text:
How does feedback guide the next action?

LOOP ENGINEERING
15

Desired state
Goal and limits

Gap

Controller
Choose one correction

Actuator
Apply the correction

System
Code and runtime

Sensor
Measure the changed system
Observed
output
Measured state and failed requirements
New code, new documents, or changed model behavior can disturb the result.
notes:
Start on the left with the desired state: what we want to be true.
The controller chooses a correction. The actuator applies it to the system.
The system then produces a new result. The sensor measures that result and sends the evidence back.
We compare what happened with what we wanted. That difference guides the next decision.
This is feedback. We are choosing the next action using the result of the last one.
Next slide:
What fills each of these boxes in our support-assistant example?
Presenter cue:
Trace the top path first, then the return path from the System output through the Sensor.

title: 1. The sensor
text:
1. The sensor

LOOP ENGINEERING
17
What does the loop need to see first?
Save the evidence that makes a failure understandable.
Observe
Save the question, search query, sources, and answer.

Check
Compare the retrieved sources with the expected article.

Report
Keep the failed case so the next attempt can use it.
notes:
The first step is to make the problem visible.
An answer can go wrong before the model writes a sentence. The search may already have lost the information it needs.
We save the input, the actual search query, the returned sources, and the answer.
That gives the next attempt a specific failure to work on.
Next slide:
What did the search actually receive for our follow-up question?

title: What did the search actually receive?
text:
What did the search actually receive?

LOOP ENGINEERING
18
The follow-up reached search without the earlier topic.
notes:
Here is the earlier question about duplicate webhook deliveries.
The follow-up is simply, ‘What should I do next?’
Now look at the query sent to search. It contains only that short follow-up.
The expected webhook article is missing from the returned sources. We now have a concrete place to investigate.
Next slide:
How do we fix this while keeping the questions that already work?
Presenter cue:
Switch to the controller. Select run 1, Before the proposed change, and D03. Collapse the patch while diagnosing the failure. Show the input, query, and sources. Open the matching trace in LangSmith if it is ready.

title: 2. Regression protection
text:
2. Regression protection

LOOP ENGINEERING
19
What must keep working after a change?
Use the same checks before and after each attempt.
Before
Save which questions pass and which fail.

Protect
Keep every question that already passes.

Separate
Keep the checker outside the agent’s edit scope.
notes:
Before making a change, we save which questions pass and which fail.
Then we use the same checks afterward.
A useful fix must preserve the existing passes, and the product tests must still pass.
We keep the questions and the checking rule outside the agent's edit scope.
Next slide:
What information does each saved question need?

title: What does a check need for each question?
text:
What does a check need for each question?

LOOP ENGINEERING
20
Pair each question with the approved article it should find.
Pass: the expected article ranks first in all three retrieval checks.
Use six questions to guide changes. Keep three other questions for a final check.
Review answer quality separately from this search check.
Question type | Expected article
Follow-up about duplicate webhooks | kb_42: webhook delivery guide
Follow-up about SSO verification | kb_14: domain verification guide
Follow-up about knowledge access | kb_31: collection access rules
notes:
Each example contains the customer's question and the approved article we expect it to find.
For a follow-up, we also keep the earlier message.
Our rule is simple: the expected article must rank first in all three retrieval checks.
We use six questions to guide the change. Three other questions stay outside the repair task and get checked after the patch is frozen.
We will still read the answer separately.
Next slide:
Once we have this evidence, which problem should the agent work on first?
Presenter cue:
Switch to development.json and point to question, followUp, and expectedSource. Show how an existing passing question stays in the comparison. Keep the final-check questions out of the repair prompt.

title: 3. The controller
text:
3. The controller

LOOP ENGINEERING
21
Which problem should the agent work on next?
Turn one failed check into a small, testable job.
Select
Choose one failed question and its evidence.

Explain
Ask what shared cause could explain the failure.

Limit
Name the files the agent may change.
notes:
The controller turns the failed checks into a small job.
It selects one failed question and gives the coding agent the relevant evidence.
The agent investigates the cause within the allowed files.
The runner then checks the proposed change using the rules we set before the repair began.
Next slide:
What clue appears in more than one of our failed questions?

title: What do the failed questions have in common?
text:
What do the failed questions have in common?

LOOP ENGINEERING
22
D01: knowledge access
D03: webhook deliveries
Both reach search as:
“What should I do next?”
Inspect how the earlier user topic reaches the search query.
The runner selected D01 first. D03 shows the same missing-context clue.
notes:
The recorded run selected D01, which concerns knowledge access.
The webhook question, D03, gives us another useful example of the same pattern.
Both reach search as, ‘What should I do next?’ even though the customer is asking about different topics.
That points us toward how the earlier user message reaches the search query.
A shared cause gives us a useful repair task.
Next slide:
What may the coding agent change to test that idea?
Presenter cue:
Show D01 and D03 in the controller or recorded task evidence. Be clear that D01 was selected first. Ask learners what information is missing from both queries before showing the patch.

title: 4. The actuator
text:
4. The actuator

LOOP ENGINEERING
23
How does the next idea become a code change?
Give Codex a bounded task in a separate worktree.
Skill
Describe the intended behavior with a reviewed example.

Scope
Allow RAG code and focused regression tests.

Output
Return a small patch for the runner to check.
notes:
The actuator is the part that turns the task into a code change.
Here, that is Codex with the repair skill, working in a separate copy of the repository.
It may change the named RAG files and add focused tests.
The questions, expected sources, models, and checking rules stay fixed.
Next slide:
What did the proposed correction actually change?

title: What did the small correction change?
text:
What did the small correction change?

LOOP ENGINEERING
24
Keep the earlier user question when building the search query.
Can change: RAG code and focused regression tests.
Keep fixed: questions, approved sources, models, and checks.
notes:
The change restores the earlier user topic when the system builds a follow-up search query.
It is a small change to how the pipeline uses the conversation.
The agent also adds tests for the context behavior, a standalone question, and the explicit option to leave context out.
When we inspect the later query, we can see the earlier topic reaching search.
Now we need to check the whole system around that change.
Next slide:
Who carries the patch through those checks without us prompting every handoff?
Presenter cue:
Open the actual patch and focused tests. Switch D03 to After the proposed change and show the combined query. The recorded repair succeeded on the first candidate. It contains no demonstrated rejected repair.

title: 5. Workflow execution
text:
5. Workflow execution

LOOP ENGINEERING
25
Who carries the work from one attempt to the next?
Let the runner handle the work between decisions.
Run
Measure, request a patch, and rerun the fixed checks.

Decide
Reject a bad patch. Hold a useful patch for review.

Remember
Save the evidence, patch, and reason for the decision.
notes:
The runner connects the work between decisions.
It measures the starting state, requests a patch, runs the product tests, and checks the questions again.
It saves the results and the current state.
A bad proposal can lead to another attempt within the limits. A useful proposal waits for review.
Next slide:
Which of those handoffs happened in this actual run?

title: What did the runner do without another prompt?
text:
What did the runner do without another prompt?

LOOP ENGINEERING
26

Measure
Same question set

Repair
One shared cause

Recheck
Tests and questions

Review
Engineer decides
The runner carried each check and handoff forward.
notes:
Follow the saved history from the first measurement.
The runner selected a failure, checked the allowed changes, ran the product tests, and repeated the question checks.
It also checked the reserved questions after the patch was fixed.
Then it paused for engineering review.
Those handoffs followed the instructions we gave at the start. We did not have to write a new prompt for each one.
Next slide:
What can a reviewer add that these checks cannot decide on their own?
Presenter cue:
Switch to the controller event history and full question table. Point to preserved passes as well as repaired questions. This run used one candidate. Explain retry behavior as supported behavior, not as an event in this recording.

title: 6. Human feedback
text:
6. Human feedback

LOOP ENGINEERING
27
What can a reviewer add to the next attempt?
Keep a clear decision and a reason the next run can use.
Review
Read the saved answer, patch, and check results.

Explain
Write the reason for a requested change.

Reuse
Add approved implementation guidance to feedback.md.
notes:
A reviewer can tell us whether the proposed behavior makes sense and what the checks have missed.
We read the patch and its evidence. We review the saved answer as a separate question.
If the review produces a reusable lesson, we write the approved guidance in feedback.md.
The next repair prompt reads that file.
That handoff is explicit. Saving a review reason alone does not update the repair guidance.
Next slide:
What would we inspect before making that decision?

title: What should a reviewer decide?
text:
What should a reviewer decide?

LOOP ENGINEERING
28
Code decision
Accept this patch as the next local baseline, or explain a rejection.

Answer quality has its own review. This record does not approve a release.
notes:
I would check whether the change preserves normal questions, uses the right user context, and keeps the existing checks intact.
The saved rehearsal records Codex as an automated engineering reviewer. The record keeps the reviewer and the reason visible.
In a live run, the responsible engineer records their own decision after reading the patch and the checks.
Acceptance makes the measured version the next local starting point.
Before resolving the review, let us look at what happens if another question arrives.
Next slide:
Should that new question interrupt a change that is still waiting for review?
Presenter cue:
Show the engineering review and its reviewer type. For a fresh live rehearsal, inspect the pending patch but leave the decision open until the flow-control application on slide 30. Show the separate answer-review form without submitting a prepared verdict.

title: 7. Flow control
text:
7. Flow control

LOOP ENGINEERING
29
When should the loop run, wait, or stop?
Watch for new work and respect an unfinished review.
Watch
Notice changes to the source or question set.

Pause
Wait while a proposed patch needs review.

Resume
After review, measure the complete question set again.
notes:
The watcher looks for new work, but it respects the current review.
If a patch is waiting for a decision, new questions can queue up. The loop waits before making more model calls.
Once the review is resolved, it measures all active questions using the selected version of the code.
If there is a failure, it has evidence for another bounded repair. If the checks pass, it waits for changed inputs.
Next slide:
Can we see that happen when a new question arrives after review?

title: What happens when a new question arrives?
text:
What happens when a new question arrives?

LOOP ENGINEERING
30

Resolve the review
Keep the decision and reason

Add a new question
A usage-export follow-up

Check all eight
Continue from the new state
pnpm rag:demo watch --id [workshop-01]
The new set passed. The watcher waited. No extra patch was needed.
notes:
The first run checked six questions and proposed the shared correction.
A seventh question arrived while the review was open, so the runner waited.
After the review decision, we added a new question about choosing dates for a complete monthly usage export.
The watcher noticed the changed question set and checked all eight active questions.
The current pipeline handled them, so it made no extra code change. With unchanged inputs, the next watch pass made no model calls.
The loop took over the fresh check and the decision to wait.
Next slide:
After the break, we will use this same idea to choose a task from your own work.

title: How can we tell whether a loop will help?
text:
How can we tell whether a loop will help?

LOOP ENGINEERING
33
Can we check progress?
A fixed test, benchmark, or reviewed answer.
Does another attempt help?
The last result tells us what to try next.
Can we contain the work?
A small change, a stop rule, and a reviewer.
notes:
Ask three questions about that task.
Can we check whether it is improving? Does the last result help choose the next attempt? Can we contain the change and stop?
If a task is unclear, we can often make it more useful by narrowing it.
Let's try those questions on a familiar case.
Next slide:
Would you let a loop work on a slow test suite?

title: Would you loop on a slow test suite?
text:
Would you loop on a slow test suite?

LOOP ENGINEERING
34
20% faster
Same tests. Same assertions. Same runner.
Can we check progress?
Compare the median of 3 full runs.

Does another attempt help?
Profile the next slow cause after each change.

Can we contain the work?
Small setup changes. Stop for review.
Run a goal and follow the timing evidence.
notes:
This is a useful fit when we protect the tests and use a repeatable measurement.
The timing profile gives the agent a next place to look.
The same suite tells us whether that change helped.
A small scope and a review point let us contain the work.
Next slide:
Would we give a documentation loop the same freedom?

title: How much of docs maintenance can run alone?
text:
How much of docs maintenance can run alone?

LOOP ENGINEERING
35
Verified facts only
Every wording change must match shipped behavior.
Can we check progress?
Build and link checks help. Meaning needs review.

Does another attempt help?
Fix the next confirmed mismatch in the list.

Can we contain the work?
Docs-only diff. Leave unclear claims for a person.
Automate verified edits. Review the product meaning.
notes:
A documentation loop can find a verified mismatch, update it, and rerun the build and link checks.
Those checks are useful, but they cannot fully decide whether a product claim is true.
We can let the loop work through confirmed edits while unclear claims wait for a person.
The review boundary follows what our checks can actually establish.
Next slide:
What happens if the request gives us no shared way to recognise a good change?

title: Would you loop on “make the UX better”?
text:
Would you loop on “make the UX better”?

LOOP ENGINEERING
36
What counts as done?
The request gives the agent no shared finish line.
Can we check progress?
No agreed user task or acceptance check.

Does another attempt help?
More edits can simply create more disagreement.

Can we contain the work?
The request could change any product journey.
Rewrite: fix one ticket-search keyboard trap and verify focus + Escape.
notes:
‘Make the whole UX better’ leaves too much undecided.
We have no agreed user task or check. Another edit may simply create another opinion.
Now narrow the request to one keyboard trap in ticket search.
We can check where focus moves and whether Escape behaves as expected.
The smaller task gives the loop a clearer next action and a visible finish line.

Slides 38 to 41 form the four-slide learner exercise. Learners move to their editor, terminal, controller, or replay. Use the prepared RAG or replay path as the default when setup time is limited. Use a fresh ID for live experiments.

title: What instructions does your loop need?
text:
What instructions does your loop need?

Replace every highlighted field with a detail from your own task.

39
Goal
/goal Reach [a result you can check].
Trigger
Start when [the trigger happens].

Inspect [the current evidence].

notes:

Next slide:
Could these instructions let a bad change appear successful?
Presenter cue:
Allow about three minutes to draft. RAG learners can describe the existing runner's agreement instead of starting a second controller around it. Replay learners write the same agreement from the evidence.

title: What could make a bad change pass?
text:
What could make a bad change pass?

Compare the instructions, then inspect a partner’s prompt.
LOOP ENGINEERING
40
Unclear request
“Make the tests faster
until they look good.”

A request we can check
/goal Make the full suite [20%] faster.
Compare the median of [3] full runs.
Keep every test and assertion.
Stop after [3 changes] or [25 minutes].
Leave the diff for review.

Ask a partner: what would reject a bad change?
notes:
Swap your instructions with a partner.
Ask how the agent could reach the target for the wrong reason.
Could it remove an assertion? Could it change the expected source? Could it skip the check?
Now point to the instruction or external check that would reject that change.
Next slide:
What will you save from the run so someone else can inspect the decision?
Presenter cue:
Allow about three minutes for the partner review. A useful answer identifies both a possible false pass and the check that would reject it.

Which work did the loop take over, and which decision stayed with you?
Presenter cue:
Allow a short working period, such as ten minutes. A fresh live run may still be working when that period ends. Save its real state or use the replay. The completion artifact is the evidence and next decision, not a forced passing result.

title: What work did your loop take over?
text:
What work did your loop take over?

LOOP ENGINEERING
42
What ran on its own?
Name one check or handoff you no longer had to prompt.

What changed the next action?
Point to the result the loop used.

What would make it run again?
Name the next question, changed input, or review decision.
notes:
Tell us one check or handoff that continued without another prompt.
Show the result that changed the next action.
Then name the input that would make the loop run again.
This makes the value concrete: we can point to the work the loop carried forward and the decision a person still owned.
Next slide:
Which small piece of repeated work will you automate next?
Presenter cue:
Invite two or three learners to share briefly. If a learner used the replay, ask them to explain the next action for a genuinely new failing question before discussing the answer.
Learner check:
A new question finds the expected article, but the answer leaves out an important deadline. What should this loop record, and what should a person review?
Pause for about one minute before discussing the answer.
Expected reasoning:
The source-ranking check can pass while the answer still needs a failing human quality review. Save the answer and its missing detail. Investigate the cause before approving any repair guidance. A correct source rank alone does not authorize the loop to label the answer correct.

title: What will you automate next?
text:

Give it a check and a clear boundary.
Let the evidence guide the next action.
Review the change. Then let new work start the loop again.
notes:
We started with a follow-up question that created another round of checking and prompting.
We now have an explicit path from that evidence to a change, a review, and the next input.
Choose one piece of repeated work. Give it a check you trust and a clear boundary.
Review what happens. Then decide when new work should start the loop again.
